final_message:
Subject: Town on Thursday

Dear Marcus,

I meant to write you sooner, but the week got away from me. I went to town on Thursday, and it turned out to be a much longer trip than I planned, so I will tell you how it went.

I started out early with the wagon, thinking I would be home by noon. The road was bad after the rain, and about halfway in the old mare decided she had done enough and stopped to rest. I have learned not to argue with her. We sat a good while, and then she went on as if nothing had happened.

The first person I met at the store was Mr. Haskell, who you will remember from the spring meeting. He is a very resourceful man, and he had a notion about the fence posts we were short on. It seems a fellow out past the creek has more cedar than he knows what to do with and wants to be rid of it cheap. Mr. Haskell offered to ride out with me on Saturday and see the lot. I said I would think it over, but I expect I shall go.

Then, as I was loading the flour and the lamp oil, a little girl came up and asked if I was the one who had the books. She could not have been more than ten, and she had no hat, though the wind was cold. Her name was Nell, and her grandmother had sent her to ask if I had any old almanacs to spare. I had two in the wagon, so I gave her both. You would have thought I had handed her a fortune. She thanked me three times and then ran off down the street with them held tight against her coat.

The last person I met was the postmaster, who kept me talking nearly an hour. He had a great deal to say about the new schedule and none of it kind. I did get your letter out of him, which was something, and I read it on the way home. The mare stopped again at the same place, so I read it twice.

I think the cedar posts are worth a look, and I would like your opinion before Saturday if you can spare it. If you have a spare hour, come out and ride along. Mr. Haskell would be glad of the company, and I would too.

Write when you can.

Yours,
[name]
